title: Numbers every engineer should know
scopeHtml: Scope: latency table, component throughput, data sizes, nines, using numbers to reject designs.

notes.title: Why memorise these numbers
notes.html:
Good design means knowing, roughly, how slow each operation is. If you know a network round trip inside a data centre costs 0.5 ms and a disk seek on a spinning drive costs 10 ms, you instantly see why a design with 20 sequential remote calls is slow. These numbers are approximate and change with hardware; the orders of magnitude are what matter.

The table below follows the classic "latency numbers every programmer should know" idea (popularised by Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig), with modern rounding. Treat values as ballpark and confirm for your hardware.

Worked example. A page needs 50 sequential cache lookups. At 0.5 ms each that is 25 ms, fine. The same 50 calls to a DB at 5 ms each is 250 ms, painful. Batching into one multi-get call turns 50 round trips into 1.

Industry examples. Facebook's memcache paper describes batching and parallelising lookups for exactly this reason. Google's search fans out queries and cares about tail latency for the same reason.

Everyday analogy. Fetching from your desk (cache), the next room (RAM), another building (SSD), another city (network far away).

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting numbers as exact; say "about", and show you know the orders of magnitude.
  • Not using the numbers to reject a design.

notes.title: Latency table
notes.html:
Approximate, modern hardware.

Operation                                     Time
-----------------------------------------------------------
L1 cache reference                            ~1 ns
Branch mispredict                             ~3 ns
L2 cache reference                            ~4 ns
Mutex lock/unlock                             ~25 ns
Main memory (RAM) reference                   ~100 ns
Compress 1 KB with a fast codec (Snappy/LZ4)  ~2-10 us
Send 1 KB over 1 Gbps network                 ~10 us
Read 4 KB random from NVMe SSD                ~20-100 us
Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM               ~10-50 us
Round trip within same data centre            ~0.5 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD               ~0.1-1 ms
HDD seek                                      ~5-10 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from HDD               ~2-10 ms
Round trip same region, different zone        ~1-2 ms
Round trip US coast to coast                  ~60-70 ms
Round trip Europe to US                       ~80-120 ms
Round trip India to US                        ~200-300 ms

Decision gravity. Latency budgets are architectural: choosing a multi-region synchronous write (adds 100+ ms to every write) is a hard-to-reverse choice because clients and SLAs assume it. Choosing async replication trades latency for possible data loss on failover.

Worked example. User in Mumbai, servers in Virginia: 250 ms round trip. TLS handshake plus request is 2 to 3 round trips on first connect, so 500 to 750 ms before any content. Fix: CDN or edge region in Mumbai, connection reuse, HTTP/3.

Industry examples. Cloudflare and Akamai exist because the speed of light is fixed. AWS offers Mumbai and Hyderabad regions for the same reason.

Everyday analogy. A letter to the neighbour versus a letter overseas: the postman is fast, the distance is not.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that cross-region calls are 100 times slower than in-DC calls.
  • Assuming SSD removes the need for caching; RAM is still 100x faster than a 100 us SSD read.

notes.title: Throughput and capacity of common components
notes.html:
Rough per-node capacities. Always say "assume" and verify by load test.

Component                      Rough per-node capacity
--------------------------------------------------------------
Web/app server (simple API)    ~1K-10K req/s (depends on work)
NGINX static/proxy             ~10K-50K+ req/s (small responses)
Redis (single instance)        ~100K ops/s (simple), more with pipelining
Memcached                      ~100K-1M ops/s per node (multi-threaded)
PostgreSQL / MySQL (primary)   ~1K-10K write TPS; ~10K-50K simple reads/s
Cassandra / DynamoDB-style     ~10K-50K writes/s per node, scale linearly
Kafka (per broker)             ~100-500 MB/s; per partition ~10-50 MB/s
Elasticsearch node             ~1K-5K search QPS (query dependent)
10 Gbps NIC                    ~1.25 GB/s
SSD (NVMe)                     ~1-3 GB/s sequential, 100K-500K IOPS
HDD                            ~100-200 MB/s sequential, ~100-200 IOPS

Worked example. 350,000 peak read QPS and a 95% cache hit ratio: DB sees 17,500 reads/s. One Postgres node is borderline; three read replicas are comfortable. With Redis at 100K ops/s per node you need 4 nodes (plus replicas) for cache.

Industry examples. Redis's own benchmark docs show 100K+ ops/s on one core. LinkedIn published Kafka numbers of millions of messages/s on a modest cluster; Kafka's strength is sequential disk I/O and batching.

Decision gravity. Picking a database by throughput ceiling is a one-way door: moving from single Postgres to a sharded system later means re-keying data. Pick the ceiling you need for the next 2 to 3 years, not for 10.

Everyday analogy. Counter capacities: a cash till does 1 customer per minute, a self-checkout bank handles 10 at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Stating that "MongoDB does 1M ops/s" without hardware and workload.
  • Ignoring that writes with fsync, indexes or secondary indexes are far slower than the headline.

notes.title: Data size cheat sheet
notes.html:
Know typical object sizes so storage estimates are one line.

Item                               Size
---------------------------------------------
Integer ID (int64)                 8 B
UUID                               16 B (binary) / 36 B (text)
Timestamp                          8 B
Tweet / short chat message         100-300 B
Small DB row (user)                ~0.5-1 KB
JSON API response (typical)        1-10 KB
Web page (HTML only)               50-100 KB
Photo, compressed (phone)          1-3 MB
Thumbnail                          10-50 KB
Music track (MP3 ~4 min)           ~4 MB
Video, 1 min, 720p                 ~20-30 MB (about 3 Mbps)
Video, 1 min, 1080p                ~40-60 MB (about 5-8 Mbps)
Log line                           100-500 B

Worked example. 500M log lines/day x 300 B = 150 GB/day; 30 days is 4.5 TB. Compression (4x typical for text logs) brings it to about 1.1 TB.

Worked example. 1 hour of 1080p video at 6 Mbps = 6 x 3600 / 8 = 2.7 GB. A platform receiving 500 hours of video per minute (YouTube has quoted figures of this order) ingests about 1.35 TB/min before transcoding into multiple renditions.

Industry examples. Netflix stores many renditions of each title (different bitrates and codecs), multiplying raw size by 10 or more. WhatsApp compresses media before upload to save both bandwidth and storage.

Everyday analogy. Knowing a suitcase weighs 20 kg so a car boot holds five.

Common interview traps.

  • Using decimal vs binary units inconsistently (not worth fighting over).
  • Forgetting multiple renditions and thumbnails for media.

notes.title: Availability, time and handy powers
notes.html:
Memorise nines, seconds in a period and powers of two.

Availability   Downtime per year   per month   per day
---------------------------------------------------------
99%            3.65 days           7.2 h       14.4 min
99.9%          8.76 h              43.8 min    1.44 min
99.99%         52.6 min            4.4 min     8.6 s
99.999%        5.26 min            26 s        0.86 s

Powers of two:
2^10 = 1 thousand (KB)   2^20 = 1 million (MB)   2^30 = 1 billion (GB)
2^40 = 1 trillion (TB)   2^50 = 1 quadrillion (PB)
2^32 = 4.3 billion       2^64 ~ 1.8 x 10^19
Seconds/day 86,400   Seconds/year ~31.5M

Worked example. A service called in a chain of 5 dependencies each at 99.9% has combined availability of 0.999^5 = 99.5%, about 1.8 days of downtime a year, worse than any single piece. Redundancy and timeouts matter because availability multiplies.

Industry examples. AWS S3 is designed for 99.99% availability and 11 nines of durability (durability and availability are different things). Google's SRE book argues for choosing an SLO below 100% on purpose.

Decision gravity. The target number is a business decision with cost steps: going from 99.9% to 99.99% typically means multi-AZ with automated failover (reversible, moderate cost); 99.999% usually means multi-region active-active (hard to undo, large cost).

Everyday analogy. Nines are like how few days a year the lift can be broken: one day a month is very different from one hour a year.

Common interview traps.

  • Promising "five nines" without costing it.
  • Mixing availability with durability.
  • Forgetting that dependency chains multiply failure.

notes.title: Using the numbers to reject bad designs
notes.html:
Run the numbers to kill ideas quickly. A few reflexes:

  • "Sequential calls": N calls x latency. 100 calls to another service at 2 ms is 200 ms; use batching or parallel calls.
  • "Read from disk per request": a 10 ms HDD seek caps one disk at about 100 requests/s; use cache or SSD.
  • "Cross-region on the hot path": adds 100+ ms; use regional replicas.
  • "Store everything in one DB row/table": 10 TB in one Postgres is possible but backup and restore take hours (at 200 MB/s, 10 TB is about 14 hours); plan sharding or tiering.
  • "Send big files through app servers": each upload occupies a connection and bandwidth; use pre-signed URLs.

Worked example. Product page budget 300 ms. Calls: auth (5 ms), catalog (10 ms), price (10 ms), reviews (20 ms), recommendations (80 ms). In parallel, the page costs about 80 ms plus overhead; sequential it is 125 ms. Both fit, but a cross-region recommendation call at 150 ms would break it, so cache or colocate.

Industry examples. Amazon famously measured that every extra 100 ms of latency cost sales (widely quoted); Google reported similar findings for search. Hence the latency budget culture.

Everyday analogy. A commute plan: if each leg takes 20 minutes and you have three legs in series, you cannot reach work in 30.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "it will be fast" with no arithmetic.
  • Treating parallel and sequential calls as equal.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Know the latency ladder: ns (CPU), 100 ns (RAM), 100 us (SSD), 0.5 ms (same DC), 10 ms (HDD seek), 100+ ms (cross-region).
  • Per-node throughput: app 1K to 10K, Redis 100K, SQL 10K reads, Kafka hundreds of MB/s. Always "assume, then load test".
  • Data sizes: ID 8 B, row 1 KB, photo 2 MB, 1080p minute 50 MB.
  • Nines: 99.9% = 8.8 h/year, 99.99% = 53 min/year; chained dependencies multiply.
  • Use numbers to reject designs: sequential calls, cross-region hot paths, disk per request, big files through app servers.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the latency numbers you keep in your head and how you use them in a design.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who know orders of magnitude reject bad designs in seconds. It separates arithmetic reasoning from name-dropping.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: About: L1 cache 1 ns, RAM 100 ns, NVMe read 20 to 100 us, same-datacentre round trip 0.5 ms, HDD seek 5 to 10 ms, cross-region 60 to 250 ms. Each step is roughly 10x to 1000x slower, and network hops dominate in-memory work. I use them to count sequential calls and multiply.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ns        us         ms              100ms+
RAM ---> SSD ---> same-DC RTT ---> HDD seek ---> cross-region
100 ns   ~50 us    0.5 ms         5-10 ms        60-250 ms

Use: operations x latency = budget. 50 sequential cache calls at 0.5 ms = 25 ms; 50 sequential DB calls at 5 ms = 250 ms. Batching to one multi-get turns 50 round trips into 1. The numbers are hardware-dependent; quote "about" and show the orders of magnitude.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting them as exact.
  • Not using them to reject anything.
  • Forgetting cross-region calls are ~100x in-DC calls.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does SSD remove the need for a cache? -> No, RAM is still ~100x faster than a 100 us SSD read.
  2. Why does TLS hurt far users? -> 2 to 3 round trips on first connect, 250 ms RTT means 500 to 750 ms before content.
  3. What is tail latency amplification? -> A fan-out to N services waits for the slowest; p99 of the whole is much worse than p99 of one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE recites the table. Senior converts it to a per-request budget and picks batching, parallelism or colocation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An N+1 query loop looked fine in staging (same host) and cost seconds in production with a cross-AZ database.

questions.promptHtml: What do "three nines" and "four nines" mean in downtime, and what does each extra nine cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: SLAs are product promises. A senior can translate them to downtime and cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: 99.9% is about 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes, 99.999% about 5 minutes. Each extra nine multiplies cost and complexity: 99.9% to 99.99% is typically multi-AZ with automated failover; 99.999% usually needs multi-region active-active.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
99%     3.65 days/yr   14.4 min/day
99.9%   8.76 h/yr      1.44 min/day
99.99%  52.6 min/yr    8.6 s/day
99.999% 5.26 min/yr    0.86 s/day

Availability multiplies along a chain: 5 dependencies at 99.9% each give 0.999^5 = 99.5%. Availability is not durability: S3 is designed for 99.99% availability and 11 nines of durability, different promises. At 99.99% you have about 4.4 minutes per month, less than most human on-call response, so recovery must be automated.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Promising five nines without costing it.
  • Confusing availability with durability.
  • Ignoring dependency chains.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you improve a chain? -> Remove serial dependencies, add redundancy, timeouts, degrade gracefully.
  2. Why choose an SLO below 100%? -> It buys feature velocity (error budget) and 100% is unreachable.
  3. Planned maintenance counts? -> Depends on the SLA definition; clarify.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE memorises the table. Senior links the nine to architecture steps, the 5-minute response problem and the error budget.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "four nines" contract was signed on top of a single-region database with a 30-minute manual failover.

questions.promptHtml: Give rough per-node capacities for common components, and explain how you use them without sounding like you are guessing.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Capacity decisions need defensible numbers; interviewers listen for "assume, then load test".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: App server about 1K to 10K requests/s depending on work, Redis about 100K ops/s per instance, Postgres or MySQL primary about 1K to 10K write TPS and 10K to 50K simple reads/s, Kafka hundreds of MB/s per broker, NVMe 100K to 500K IOPS. I always say "assume" and add that I would load test, because workload and fsync and indexes change it by an order of magnitude.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Use the numbers to size tiers: 350K peak reads/s with 95% cache hit leaves 17.5K for the DB. One Postgres node is borderline, so three replicas. Redis at 100K/s needs about 4 nodes plus replicas. A headline benchmark depends on payload size, number of indexes, durable writes (fsync), network and batching. "MongoDB does 1M ops/s" is meaningless without hardware and workload. Pick the DB by the ceiling you need for the next 2 to 3 years; moving later is a one-way door.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting vendor headline numbers.
  • Ignoring write amplification from secondary indexes.
  • Sizing for 10 years.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Kafka fast? -> Sequential disk I/O, batching, page cache, zero-copy.
  2. A DB at 10K reads/s but you need 50K? -> Cache, then replicas.
  3. How do you verify the number? -> Load test with production-like data, queries and concurrency, watch p99 not average.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE states a number. Senior states the assumption, the drivers that move it and the test.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration to a "1M ops/s" store was sized on a benchmark with 100 B values; real values were 8 KB and throughput fell 20x.

questions.promptHtml: Which object sizes do you memorise for storage estimation, and how do you turn them into a capacity number?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Estimation speed shows engineering maturity, and the easy-to-miss multipliers (renditions, replicas) matter.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ID 8 B, UUID 16 B binary, small row about 1 KB, short message 100 to 300 B, compressed photo 1 to 3 MB, thumbnail 10 to 50 KB, one minute of 1080p about 50 MB. Storage per day is count x size, then multiply by replicas, renditions and retention.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: 500M log lines/day x 300 B = 150 GB/day; 30 days = 4.5 TB; text compresses ~4x to ~1.1 TB; with 3 replicas ~3.4 TB. Video: 1 hour at 6 Mbps = 6 x 3600 / 8 = 2.7 GB. 500 hours uploaded per minute is about 1.35 TB per minute before transcoding into many renditions, which can multiply raw size 10x or more.

daily count x size x replicas x renditions x retention

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting replication factor and thumbnails/renditions.
  • Mixing bits and bytes (Mbps vs MB).
  • Ignoring index size, often 30 to 100% of the table.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Bits vs bytes? -> Mbps /8 is MB/s.
  2. How do you cut storage cost? -> Compression, tiering to cold storage, dedup, retention policy.
  3. How big are the indexes? -> Estimate per index entry size x rows; they also need RAM.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE computes raw size. Senior includes replication, renditions, index, growth and the cost line.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A photo feature budgeted 2 MB per upload and forgot four thumbnail sizes and three copies, tripling the storage bill.

questions.contextHtml: A product page endpoint makes these calls one after another: auth 5 ms, catalog 10 ms, price 10 ms, reviews 20 ms, recommendations 80 ms, and then 50 individual cache lookups for related items at 0.5 ms each. Budget is 300 ms p99 end to end. Today it measures 190 ms at p50 but 480 ms at p99. Recommendations is now served from a service in another region at 150 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Where does the time go, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add caching" with no accounting of what is sequential, or blames the slowest call only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which calls depend on each other? Is the cross-region call required on the hot path? What does stale data cost for recommendations?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a timeout and a fallback (empty or cached recommendations) on the slow call.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Sequential chain: 5+10+10+20+150+25 = 220 ms at p50-ish, tails add up; cross-region recommendations; 50 cache lookups sequential cost 25 ms.
  4. How I'd verify: Tracing spans per call; compare sum of spans to wall time.
  5. Root cause: Serial execution plus a 150 ms cross-region dependency.
  6. Fix: Run catalog, price, reviews and recommendations in parallel after auth: cost becomes max, about 150 ms, then 5 ms for auth, total about 160 ms. Replace the 50 lookups with one multi-get (0.5 ms). Replicate or cache recommendations in region (about 10 ms), leaving the parallel max about 20 ms, total about 30 ms.
  7. Prevention: Latency budget per dependency; trace-based regression alerts.
  8. Trade-offs: Parallel calls raise peak load on dependencies and make p99 depend on the slowest; fallbacks mean sometimes stale recommendations, which I accept for a product page but not for price.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Price depends on catalog? -> Then catalog then price are serial, the rest stay parallel.
  • Fan-out to 10 services in parallel? -> Tail latency grows; use hedged requests or tight timeouts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A page dropped from 900 ms to 120 ms by one multi-get and a parallel fan-out, without touching a database.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a cache blindly.
  • Hire: sums the chain, parallelises, batches.
  • Strong hire: handles cross-region dependency, timeouts, tail amplification.

questions.contextHtml: Platform engineering asks for a storage and cost plan for centralised application logs. 400 services, together 600M log lines per day, average 350 B per line, 30 days hot retention, 1 year cold. Replication factor 2 on the hot tier. Hot tier costs about 10x per GB compared with cold. The CFO flinches at the first number you say.
questions.promptHtml: Estimate storage and propose how to bring cost down.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Computes raw size only, ignores replication and compression, offers no levers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are logs searched after 7 days? Are there compliance retention rules? Is there debug-level noise? Peak vs average ingest?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop DEBUG in production and sample health-check logs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Largest cost is the hot tier; noise logs; no compression.
  4. How I'd verify: Per-service volume top 10, level distribution, query access logs by age.
  5. Root cause (math): 600M x 350 B = 210 GB/day. 30 days = 6.3 TB raw. Compress 4x: ~1.6 TB. Replication 2: ~3.2 TB hot. Cold 1 year: 210 GB x 365 = 77 TB raw, ~19 TB compressed. Ingest rate ~7K lines/s average, ~2.4 MB/s, trivial; peak maybe 3x.
  6. Fix: Hot 7 days, warm 30 days, cold object storage for the rest; sample and cap per service; structured logs compress better; index only needed fields.
  7. Prevention: Per-team quotas and cost reports.
  8. Trade-offs: Shorter hot retention slows old investigations (rehydration takes minutes); sampling loses rare events, so keep errors at 100%.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compliance wants 7 years? -> Cold tier with lifecycle rules, about 130 TB per year class, check cost per GB.
  • Compression 2x not 4x? -> Redo; state assumption and measure on a real sample.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One chatty service wrote 40% of all logs because of a debug flag left on after an incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raw size only.
  • Hire: includes compression, replication, retention.
  • Strong hire: tiering, per-service quotas, validates assumptions.

questions.contextHtml: Checkout calls five services in series: auth, cart, pricing, inventory and payments. Each has a measured availability of 99.9%. The business has promised customers 99.95% for checkout. A VP says "every service is three nines, so we are fine." Payments is a third-party API at 99.9% that you cannot change.
questions.promptHtml: Are you meeting the promise? What do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts that each part meets 99.9% so the whole does.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are failures independent? Which calls are mandatory vs optional? Is the SLA measured per request or per month? Are retries safe?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; do the math first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Serial chain: 0.999^5 = 99.5%, roughly 1.8 days a year, 44 hours; below 99.95% (4.4 hours a year).
  4. How I'd verify: Compute from real error data, not designs; check correlated failures (shared DB, shared zone).
  5. Root cause: Availability multiplies along serial dependencies.
  6. Fix: Make non-critical calls optional (pricing cached, inventory soft check with later reconcile); add retry with idempotency to payments and a second PSP for failover; cache auth validation; fewer serial hops. If four are made resilient the chain may be 99.9% x payments redundancy.
  7. Prevention: Error budget per dependency, SLO alerts on the end-to-end flow.
  8. Trade-offs: A second PSP costs integration and reconciliation; soft inventory checks risk overselling, so I accept a small oversell with compensation for low-value items only.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Failures correlate (same AZ)? -> The product math is optimistic; spread across zones.
  • Cannot change payments? -> Queue and retry with "pending" state to the user.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promise of four nines was met only after two optional calls were wrapped in fallbacks, lifting the real figure from 99.6%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts three nines each.
  • Hire: multiplies, finds the gap.
  • Strong hire: redundancy, optional vs critical, correlated failure caveat.

questions.contextHtml: A company serves users in Mumbai from servers in Virginia. Complaints: "first load takes 2 seconds." Measured RTT is 250 ms. Page load waterfall: DNS 250 ms, TCP 250 ms, TLS 500 ms, first byte 300 ms (including 40 ms server time), then 14 API calls over the same connection, 4 sequential. Engineering says "the servers are fast, 40 ms."
questions.promptHtml: Explain the 2 seconds and propose fixes with expected savings.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Optimises the 40 ms server time, which is not the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share of users are in India? Is content personalised or static? Can data live in region (residency)? Mobile networks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a CDN in front for static assets and terminate TLS at the edge.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Round trips, not compute: connection setup is 1 DNS + 1 TCP + 2 TLS (1.2) round trips = ~1 s; sequential API calls 4 x 250 ms = 1 s; server work only 40 ms.
  4. How I'd verify: Browser waterfall and WebPageTest from Mumbai; count round trips.
  5. Root cause: Speed of light, multiplied by round trips.
  6. Fix: Edge or Mumbai region termination cuts handshake RTT to about 20 ms; TLS 1.3 and HTTP/3 reduce round trips; connection reuse; parallelise or batch the sequential API calls (one aggregate call = 1 RTT); read replicas or regional cache for reads.
  7. Prevention: Real-user monitoring per country; latency budget on round trips.
  8. Trade-offs: A regional write path needs replication; synchronous cross-region writes add 100+ ms to every write and are hard to undo, so keep writes in one home region or use async replication with a stated loss window.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Data residency forbids replication? -> Edge only for static and TLS; regional deployment for the rest.
  • Why not just a bigger server? -> Compute is 40 ms of 2000 ms.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving TLS termination to an edge location halved perceived load time with zero backend changes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes server code.
  • Hire: counts round trips, CDN.
  • Strong hire: per-handshake accounting, batching, write-path gravity.

questions.contextHtml: The orders database is 10 TB on one Postgres primary and grows 1 TB per quarter. The RTO in the DR policy is 2 hours. Nightly full backup to object storage currently takes 11 hours. Restore on fresh hardware has never been tested. Storage throughput of restore target: about 200 MB/s. The team says "we have backups, we are safe."
questions.promptHtml: Assess the DR posture with numbers and propose a plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Trusts that backups exist; no restore-time math.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is RPO? Is there a standby? Are WAL archives kept? How compressible is the data? Is the 200 MB/s a measurement or a spec?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run a restore drill this week; set up a streaming standby.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 10 TB at 200 MB/s = 10,000,000 MB / 200 = 50,000 s, about 14 hours, 7x the RTO; the backup window of 11 hours will be 12 hours next quarter.
  4. How I'd verify: Measure restore throughput on real hardware and include index rebuild and WAL replay time.
  5. Root cause: One large database makes recovery time proportional to size.
  6. Fix: Short term: hot standby with failover (minutes) plus PITR via WAL archive; incremental/snapshot-based backups (block-level snapshots restore in minutes to start). Long term: partition by time or tenant, archive old partitions, eventually shard so each restore is smaller.
  7. Prevention: Quarterly restore drills with a recorded time; alert on backup duration growth.
  8. Trade-offs: A standby covers hardware failure but not logical corruption (a bad DELETE replicates), so keep PITR and delayed replica; sharding is a one-way door, so size partitioning first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• RPO of 1 minute? -> Synchronous or near-sync replication plus continuous WAL archiving.
  • Data doubles to 20 TB? -> Restore is 28 hours at the same speed; snapshots or sharding become mandatory.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team discovered in a drill that their "tested" backup restore needed 31 hours, after an incident would have made it a 31-hour outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: backups are enough.
  • Hire: computes 14 hours, standby, drill.
  • Strong hire: logical corruption, snapshots, partitioning, trends.

questions.contextHtml:
Peak 350,000 read QPS served by Redis (4 nodes) and one Postgres primary with 3 replicas, each replica comfortable up to about 15K reads/s. After a deploy that changed a cache key format, metrics at 20:05:

cache hit ratio: 95% -> 62%
db read qps:     17,500 -> 133,000
replica cpu:     35% -> 100%
db p99:          12 ms -> 2.4 s
app error rate:  0.1% -> 18% (timeouts)
redis cpu:       40% -> 25%

Someone suggests adding more Redis nodes.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and what do you do in the first 10 minutes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds Redis nodes or replicas, ignoring that the hit ratio fell.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly deployed at 20:00? Is the new key format readable by the old? Is cold start involved? Are retries amplifying?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the deploy; shed load (disable non-critical reads), and cap retries.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Key format change causing mass misses (the fall in hit ratio coincides); cache stampede on popular keys; eviction due to memory. Red herring: Redis CPU dropped because it serves fewer hits.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare key patterns in redis-cli monitor samples, check keyspace_misses, evicted_keys, per-key miss counts.
  5. Root cause: Math: DB load = 350K x (1 - hit). 5% miss is 17.5K, 38% miss is 133K, 7.6x the load on a tier whose three replicas total about 45K reads/s. A small drop in hit ratio causes a big DB increase.
  6. Fix: Rollback; warm the new keys gradually (dual-read old and new format), request coalescing/single-flight to stop stampedes, and jittered TTLs.
  7. Prevention: Alert on hit ratio and DB QPS, canary key-format changes with cache-hit checks, load test with cold cache.
  8. Trade-offs: More replicas would not catch 133K reads/s and only risk replication lag; I would not scale the DB for a problem that a rollback fixes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rollback also cold? -> Old keys still exist if TTL has not expired; otherwise warm from the DB in batches.
  • Planned format change? -> Versioned key prefix, dual-write, then cut over.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hit-ratio drop from 98% to 90% quadrupled DB load and caused a page; the alert on ratio alone would have fired five minutes earlier.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds nodes.
  • Hire: connects deploy to hit ratio, rolls back.
  • Strong hire: does the miss math, stampede protection, dual-read migration.

questions.contextHtml:
A video-sharing feature lets users upload files of ~200 MB through the API servers, which then write to storage. There are 20 app servers, each with a 1 Gbps NIC and 200 worker threads. At 2,000 concurrent uploads, the observed picture is:

app nic out/in: 100% / 100%
worker threads busy: 100%
login endpoint p99: 8 s
upload success: 71%

Each upload takes about 3 minutes on a typical mobile link of 10 Mbps.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the whole site slow and how would you redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds more app servers and larger instances.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do uploads need virus scanning before storage? Resumable required? What fraction of traffic is uploads vs everything else?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Isolate upload traffic onto its own pool; limit concurrent uploads per instance.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Each upload holds a connection and a thread for 3 minutes: 2,000 x 200 MB = 400 GB in flight; 2,000 uploads x 10 Mbps = 20 Gbps in aggregate, equal to the fleet's 20 Gbps NIC capacity; threads exhausted so login starves.
  4. How I'd verify: Thread dumps, per-endpoint connection counts, NIC graphs.
  5. Root cause: Large file bodies are streamed through a tier built for small API calls.
  6. Fix: Pre-signed URLs so the client uploads directly to object storage; app server only issues the URL and records metadata; multipart/resumable upload; async post-processing (scan, transcode) via a queue triggered by the storage event.
  7. Prevention: Separate pools and limits per endpoint class; load test with slow clients.
  8. Trade-offs: Direct upload shifts validation to after-the-fact, so quarantine until scanned; pre-signed URL expiry and size limits needed for security.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need to reject unauthorised files? -> Short-lived URL scoped to key, size and content type.
  • Client drops at 90%? -> Resumable multipart so only missing parts retry.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving uploads to pre-signed URLs let the API fleet shrink by half and removed a weekly "login is slow" page.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales servers.
  • Hire: pre-signed URL and async processing.
  • Strong hire: quantifies in-flight bytes, thread starvation, security and resumability.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager says: "Our new payments-adjacent API must be five nines." The service currently runs in one region across 3 AZs at about 99.9% measured. Team of 6 engineers, current infra cost about 40K per month. Revenue per minute of full outage is estimated at 800.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond, and what do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, we will make it five nines" or flatly "impossible".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Per what window and what counts as downtime (errors, latency)? Is it a contractual SLA with penalties or an aspiration? Which operations need it (the write path or reads)? Which failures matter (region loss)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reframe: nines are a business decision with cost steps.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 99.999% = 5.26 minutes a year, 26 seconds a month: below detection plus human response time; needs full automation and multi-region active-active, with dependencies (including third parties) that cannot all meet it.
  4. How I'd verify: Compute expected loss: 99.9% is 526 minutes a year x 800 = about 420K; 99.99% is 53 minutes = about 42K; five nines is about 4K. The gain from 99.99% to 99.999% is under 40K a year.
  5. Root cause: n/a; it is a requirements conversation.
  6. Fix: Propose 99.99% for the write path: multi-AZ with automated failover (reversible, moderate cost), tested failover, graceful degradation; five nines only for a narrow critical function if the contract pays for it.
  7. Prevention: Error budget policy, game days, SLO dashboards.
  8. Trade-offs: Active-active multi-region brings conflict resolution, data residency complexity and likely a 2x to 3x infra cost, a hard-to-undo architecture; I would not commit before costing it and checking the dependency chain.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The contract has penalties of 5M? -> Re-run the expected-loss math; five nines might pay.
  • Third party at 99.9%? -> The ceiling is theirs unless a fallback provider exists.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team quoted five nines, then spent a year discovering that no vendor in the chain could support it; they renegotiated to 99.95% with a degraded mode.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts or refuses without reasoning.
  • Hire: asks definitions, converts to downtime, proposes steps.
  • Strong hire: expected-loss comparison, dependency ceiling, reversibility of the architecture.
